sections.descriptionEn: In Tenants Advocacy Practicum I, students will provide information, legal advice, and representation to tenants. They will work on cases for tenants facing a wide variety of housing issues (including but not limited to habitability issues, payment disputes, lease violations, unlawful lockouts, and small claims actions) or seeking eviction defense and homelessness prevention. The students will interview tenants and conduct substantive research into the applicable law. Students will draft legal memoranda and may prepare pleadings for town, village, and city court cases. Students may have the opportunity to appear in court. The students may also circulate tenants’ rights information to the community in collaboration with local tenants' unions. The laws affecting tenants and landlords have been changing rapidly since 2019, against a backdrop of racial inequality.

sections.titleEn: International Human Rights: Litigation and Advocacy Clinic I
sections.descriptionEn: In this clinical course, students will work on projects that will expose them to diverse forms of human rights advocacy. The clinic is litigation-oriented, although clinic students may also have the opportunity to engage in fact-finding and research regarding human rights violations abroad. A current sampling of projects includes: (1) representation of women facing the death penalty around the world; (2) documenting and reporting on human rights violations in Israel and the Occupied Territories; and (3) documenting and reporting on human rights violations in the United States under the rise of authoritarianism. Interested students must submit a c.v. and statement of interest to be considered.

sections.descriptionEn: This course carries 4, 5, or 6 credits and has two required components: casework, and a lawyering seminar. Casework (2, 3, or 4 credits): Cornell Law School created this clinic because of the urgent need for legal services in the farmworker community. Employment on a farm is one of the world’s most difficult and dangerous occupations. Farmworkers experience geographic, linguistic, and cultural isolation, separation from family, immigration insecurity reinforced by policing practices, workplace sexual violence, and exclusion from coverage under certain employment laws. Working with the clinic's community partners and a clinic student partner, Farmworker Legal Assistance Clinic I student attorneys will handle deportation defense matters on behalf of individual farmworkers in the region, work that will involve intensive fact investigation and client counseling and often require litigation. As a result, the course requires off-premises travel to meet with clients and participate in hearings. Depending on requests from community partners, students may also work in brief advice and referral outreach sessions in farmworker communities. Clinic participants may also have the opportunity to work on research and writing projects with civil rights and farmworker rights organizations. Each casework credit requires 42.5 hours of casework undertaken between orientation and the end of the exam period. Lawyering Seminar (2 credits): Farmworker Clinic students will participate in a seminar focused on skills they need for effective client representation, including interviewing, counseling, fact investigation, drafting, negotiation, language accessible practice, and trial advocacy. The seminar will include readings, simulations, guest lectures, and case rounds. Notes: (1) This course may require off-premises travel. Students will be reimbursed for reasonable travel expenses. (2) All enrolled students must be available for a phone call or meeting with the clinic supervisor before the start of the semester. (3) Students must make every effort to attend a multi-clinic orientation to be scheduled within the first few weeks of the semester. Permission of instructor required. To Apply: Students will submit a resume and a brief statement of interest in the online application process. Contact the professor (Beth Lyon) with any questions about the course.

sections.descriptionEn: Permission of instructor required. Students who have completed the first semester of any clinical course, or who have significant advocacy experience, can seek the instructors' permission to enroll in Farmworker Clinic II. Applicants should submit a resume and short statement of interest (no more than one page) to Professor Beth Lyon. If you have already taken FLAC I, you may keep your statement of interest very brief and please do not mention client names. For more information about the clinic, email Prof. Lyon and schedule a meeting. Note that this course generally requires off-premises travel to meet with clients and participate in hearings. Students collaborate with farmworkers, farmworker families, and partner organizations to use the law in service of their clients' goals. FLAC II carries 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 or 6 credits, depending on the number of cases undertaken (each credit will represent 42.5 hours of casework over the course of the semester, and seminar class time will be added into those hours)

sections.titleEn: Low-Income Taxpayer Law and Accounting Practicum II
sections.descriptionEn:
This practicum equips students to master core financial and tax-literacy principles, analyze the new NIL marketplace, communicate those insights clearly, and deliver high-impact education to athletes and athletic organizations. Each participant partners with an industry professional and applies classroom learning through community-engagement projects that serve current student-athletes.
This course will take place in a shifting field of practice. For example, the landscape of college sports transformed in June 2025, when the House v. NCAA antitrust settlement opened the door for schools to direct funds to their student-athletes and hamstrung the influence of university collectives. Layer onto that a patchwork of rapidly expanding state statutes plus evolving federal proposals, and today’s student-athletes must navigate a far more complex—and opportunity-rich—financial world than their predecessors. Layer onto that a patchwork of rapidly expanding state statutes plus evolving federal proposals, and today’s student-athletes must navigate a far more complex—and opportunity-rich—financial world than their predecessors. Please write to Prof. Babcock if you are interested in taking this course.

sections.descriptionEn:
In the Tenants Advocacy Practicum II, students will continue to provide information, legal advice, and representation to tenants. Students will work on cases for tenants facing a wide variety of housing issues (including but not limited to habitability issues, payment disputes, lease violations, unlawful lockouts, and small claims actions) or seeking eviction defense and homelessness prevention.

Students will draft legal memoranda and may prepare pleadings for town, village, and city court cases. Students may have the opportunity to appear (likely virtually) in court. The students may also circulate tenants’ rights information to the community in conjunction with local tenants' unions. 

The classroom component of the course will be mostly composed of case rounds, in which students discuss their current cases with fellow students and the instructor.

sections.titleEn: Advocacy for LGBT Communities Practicum I
sections.descriptionEn: Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. This course combines fieldwork at the Volunteer Lawyers Project of CNY, Inc., in Syracuse, NY with a weekly classroom component, the scheduling of which will be a cooperative decision between the instructor and the students. Students will work on a variety of legal cases and issues that advance or defend the rights of lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) individuals and communities. Students will work on developing fundamental lawyering skills such as interviewing, client counseling, and drafting of court forms. Students will also have the opportunity to engage in public education, legal research and other advocacy. All students will work on 10-15 cases and will also be involved in additional educational/policy/advocacy projects. In the classroom sessions, cutting-edge legal issues that affect the LGBT community will be discussed including relationship and parentage recognition, discrimination, transgender rights, and asylum. The practical application of several of these issues will be discussed through development of basic lawyering skills and case strategy. Students are required to travel to the offices of the Volunteer Lawyers Project of CNY in Syracuse one day per week. Scheduling will be flexible to meet the needs of the students accepted to the course. Some course and client work can be performed remotely. Interested students are requested to submit a resume, transcript and letter of interest.
sections.additionalInformationEn: Law 7905, Advocacy for LGBT Communities Practicum, students must be available 10-4 Fridays to commute to Syracuse, NY

sections.descriptionEn: Prerequisites: Gender Justice Clinic I and permission of the instructor. Students who have completed the first semester of the Gender Justice Clinic may seek the instructors' permission to enroll in the Gender Justice Clinic II for 2, 4, or 6 credits, with credits reflecting the workload taken on. Clinic students contribute to efforts to address gender-based violence and discrimination by representing people in a variety of legal matters and undertaking advocacy projects in collaboration with community partners. Students will gain experience in legal advocacy on gender justice issues and develop lawyering and leadership skills. Students will participate in regular weekly team meetings and attend some of the seminars of the full Gender Justice Clinic. Students who wish to enroll in the Clinic should pre-register and contact Prof. Brundige to discuss their participation by the end of the pre-registration period. Supplementary application materials are not required. Please also contact Prof. Brundige if you have any questions about the course.

sections.descriptionEn: Prerequisites: Permission of the instructor required; Evidence and Criminal Procedure (Investigations) are recommended but not required. In this one-semester clinical course, students will take on the professional responsibilities of handling a criminal appeal in New York State. Students will work in pairs to review the full appellate record, research and select the most salient appealable issues, and draft the opening appellate brief on behalf of an indigent client convicted of a felony in Manhattan or the Bronx. Throughout the process, students will collaborate with their incarcerated client. The clinic partners with a holistic public defense office in New York City, so students will have the opportunity to discuss their cases with experienced appellate attorneys on a regular basis. After the clinic ends students will have the option (with instructor permission, and for experiential learning credit where applicable) of writing a reply brief and orally arguing their case in front of a five-judge panel in the Appellate Division, First Department, in Manhattan. In the course of their representation, students will learn how to: effectively and ethically communicate with clients convicted of a crime, identify and use the facts of a case to tell a compelling narrative, write persuasive and well-organized arguments that successfully integrate the facts and relevant legal authorities, and deploy effective oral advocacy in both formal and informal settings. Further, in addition to gaining knowledge of appellate procedure and doctrine and New York State criminal law, students will deepen their understanding of the U.S. criminal legal system. To apply, students should submit a resume, statement of interest, and transcript. Please contact Professor Goldberg with questions about the course, and see the clinic website for more information: https://www.lawschool.cornell.edu/academics/experiential-learning/clinical-program/appellate-criminal-defense-clinic/

sections.descriptionEn: Permission of instructor required to enroll. This ongoing practicum course represents tribes and tribal members in matters involving federal Indian law. Current cases include a claim against the Department of the Interior under The Judgment Funds Act on behalf of disenrolled members of the Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan, and the representation of the Traditional Cayuga Nation Council of Chiefs and Clan Mothers in various legal matters. Students should expect to complete myriad research and document preparation assignments related to federal court and administrative agency litigation, while concurrently developing a broad-based knowledge of voluminous historical and administrative records, which includes expert reports, research memoranda, client declarations and interview transcripts. Federal Indian Law Practicum II, III and IV are advanced courses for students who have completed previous semesters in the Practicum. These advanced clinic students are expected to take on leadership roles within the Practicum, and assist newer students with their understanding of the source material and the preparation of any documents required for the matter.

sections.descriptionEn: Prerequisite: permission of the instructor. The course will focus on fundamental investigatory and advocacy skills applicable to representation of public investors in disputes subject to arbitration at the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (f/k/a National Association of Securities Dealers), with particular attention to the elderly and small investors, and others who are not able to obtain private representation. Substantive legal topics will include the scope and nature of binding arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act and New York law, and the legal and regulatory remedies available to defrauded investors. Coursework may include training in skills such as interviewing potential clients, evaluating potential claims, preparing pleadings, conducting discovery, representing clients at hearings and negotiating settlements. Class work may include presentations by nationally-recognized experts on topics applicable to evaluation of securities accounts, trading, and products. Students may have the opportunity under faculty supervision to represent investors, to provide public education to community groups as to investment frauds, to draft position statements to regulatory authorities, and/or to participate in preparing amicus briefs, in support of public investors. Note: This course may require off premises travel for potential client and witness interviews, hearings, and community presentations. Assistance will be provided to students who lack available transportation.

Substantive legal topics will include the scope and nature of binding arbitration under the Federal Arbitration Act and New York law, and the legal and regulatory remedies available to defrauded investors. Coursework may include training in skills such as interviewing potential clients, evaluating potential claims, preparing pleadings, conducting discovery, representing clients at hearings and negotiating settlements. Class work may include presentations by nationally-recognized experts on topics applicable to evaluation of securities accounts, trading, and products. Students may have the opportunity under faculty supervision to represent investors, to provide public education to community groups as to investment frauds, to draft position statements to regulatory authorities, and/or to participate in preparing amicus briefs, in support of public investors. Note: This course may require off premises travel for potential client and witness interviews, hearings, and community presentations. Assistance will be provided to students who lack available transportation.

sections.descriptionEn: In the Veterans Law Practicum I, students will provide information, legal advice, and representation to veterans. The student work in this practicum will directly address the gaps in legal representation for veterans seeking access to various veteran-specific benefits programs. Obtaining and accessing benefits can impact the lives of veterans in many ways: by preventing homelessness, improving a veteran’s economic security and wellbeing, and providing access to medical care. Students will work on cases to secure service-connected disability compensation, discharge upgrades, overpayment issues, and other related claims. The students will interview veterans and conduct substantive research into the applicable law, including Title 38 Code of Federal Regulations, Uniform Code of Military Justice, and Federal Legislation. Students will draft legal memoranda and may prepare briefings for Veteran District Offices and/or the Board of Veterans Affairs. Students may have the opportunity to appear virtually at hearings. The students may also circulate veterans benefits information to the community in conjunction with the Tompkins County Department of Veterans Services and other stakeholders. Students will develop key lawyering skills (including interviewing, client counseling, fact investigation, drafting, and oral advocacy), gain substantive and procedural knowledge of veteran benefits laws and regulations, and engage with the ethical implications of creating an attorney-client relationship. Students are requested to submit a statement of interest.

sections.descriptionEn:
Prerequisite:  Veterans Law Practicum I and permission of the instructor.  In the Veterans Law Practicum II, students will continue advocating for veterans to obtain service-connected disability compensation, discharge upgrades, and other related claims.  Students may also perform research and draft memoranda on policy issues affecting veterans benefits programs.  The classroom component of the course will mostly consist of case rounds, in which students discuss their current cases with fellow students and with the instructor.  Advanced students will be expected to take on leadership roles within the Practicum and assist newer students with understanding the substantive and procedural issues involved in veterans advocacy.
Class time will be determined in consultation with students.
